solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Firm blood-line in doubt? I've bad news for you

indicators.note: letters whose order is in doubt are unsettled, so the fodder is to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A business worries its founding family's line of succession is uncertain, and someone breaks the grim news.
explanation.walkthrough: The thirteen letters of FIRM BLOODLINE rearrange to fill all three linked lights.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbinger of misfortune is figuratively a creature that announces trouble, so it could say these words.

clue.text: Go to someone's falling-off the-wagon party?

definitions.text: Go to someone's falling-off the-wagon party?

parts.words: Go to someone's falling-off the-wagon party?
parts.note: a teetotaller's end is the moment they fall off the wagon, and going to a party is to be present

explanation.surface: An invitation to celebrate the night someone abandons sobriety.
explanation.walkthrough: TT means teetotal, so A TT END is a teetotaller's finish, i.e. falling off the wagon; the whole is the plain verb for going to an event.
explanation.definitionFit: To be present at an event is to go to it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Sorry for one 'Giovanni' entering state of equality with Elgar

indicators.note: one piece goes into the gap between the other two, as a visitor enters a house

parts.note: par is a state of equality, as in 'on a par'
the setter's pseudonym, so the setter refers to himself as me
Mozart's Don Giovanni is one example of a don, a Spanish gentleman

explanation.surface: An apology for treating a Mozart rake as the equal of the composer Elgar.
explanation.walkthrough: Elgar is also this puzzle's setter, so 'Elgar' gives ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologetic interjection: both say you regret a small offence.

clue.text: Pop in to line up desirable young man

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
one word goes inside the other as a lining sits inside a garment

parts.note: pop is a fizzy drink, such as soda
taken as written

explanation.surface: Popping in to form a queue behind an attractive young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like a verb with 'in', but it is the fizzy drink; 'in' is a separate piece, and 'to line' puts it inside before 'up' turns the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Adonis was a strikingly beautiful youth, so the name stands for any handsome young man.

clue.text: Aldrin, say, launching 'BUZZ' (sic)?

indicators.note: in a down clue, a launch sends things upward, so the letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: the (sic) tells you to read the word exactly as printed: Buzz is a name, written here in caps

explanation.surface: An astronaut's nickname, quoted in capitals with a pedantic 'sic'.
explanation.walkthrough: NAME + CAPS is read upwards. Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon in 1969.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldrin is an example of an astronaut, here called by the old-fashioned word for a space traveller.

clue.text: One's other half's reported boost

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the word is the one that sounds like it

parts.note: one is the royal way of saying I, so the Queen's other half was her husband Prince Philip

explanation.surface: Talk of someone's spouse giving them a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Philip was the husband of Queen Elizabeth II, whose regal 'one' stands for herself.
explanation.definitionFit: A stimulus or encouragement is a synonym, as in a fillip to morale.

clue.text: When old and new collide, these people are sadly next to go

parts.note: the person next to go is the one whose ... it is
they is a pronoun for a group of people

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A grim picture of a generation clash in which the elderly are next to be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges ARE into EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: At midnight on New Year's Eve the old twelvemonth meets the new, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Dual identity assumed by poor actor's prompter

indicators.note: the jumbled word is taken into the other, as a role is taken on
dual means two copies of the abbreviation are needed

parts.note: ID is short for identity

indicators.note: poor suggests a badly made version, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A weak performer leans on cue cards while playing a double role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges the actor's letters into OTCAR, which goes inside the second of the two IDs.
explanation.definitionFit: A television presenter's cue card, held off camera, reminds the speaker of the lines, so it prompts them.

clue.text: Second fiddle varying bars

indicators.note: bars means keeps out, so these letters are removed

parts.note: something varying is inconstant
a con is a swindle or fiddle

explanation.surface: A violinist in a supporting role plays a shifting series of musical bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second fiddle' reads as one phrase; split it: 'Second' is the definition and 'fiddle' is CON.
explanation.definitionFit: A moment or very short time, as in 'wait a second'.

clue.text: Infantryman rolling up full of 'lubrication'

indicators.note: the outer letters are filled with the inner word
rolling over turns the word round

parts.note: oil is a lubricant

explanation.surface: A foot soldier rolls up after a heavy lubrication, i.e. drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Poilu was the slang name for a French infantryman in the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The French nickname for an ordinary First World War foot soldier, meaning hairy one.

clue.text: Departs NW Key, like this wordplay: part above the canal

parts.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
the Escape key sits at the top left, the north-west, of a keyboard
the wordplay before the definition finishes with a colon

explanation.surface: A cryptic remark on punctuation that ends on a colon before mentioning the canal.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay 'Departs NW Key, like this wordplay:' literally ends in a colon. The canal is the alimentary canal, ending in the anal canal.
explanation.definitionFit: This section of the large intestine runs down the left side of the abdomen, lying above the anal canal.

clue.text: Unceasingly the Barbarian performed out of church

indicators.note: letters out of the words are dropped

parts.note: Conan the Barbarian is the fictional sword-wielding hero
done means carried out or performed
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A tale of a barbarian who acted outside church without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: C and E come out of CONANDONE in order.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means continuously, without a pause, as in talking endlessly.

clue.text: See 1
Writer's last moving poem is about part-timer

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the single letter
moving letters around makes a new arrangement
the final letter of the possessive word is taken

explanation.surface: A writer's final poem stirs feelings and deals with someone who works only part of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges POEM IS into SEMIPO, which goes round the last letter taken from 'Writer'.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-professional plays or works partly for pay, alongside another job.

clue.text: See 7
Part of exercise plotting changes

parts.note: being in something means being part of it
a theme is a school composition or exercise

indicators.note: changes says the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: Something that is being reworked as plans are made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges PLOTTING into LTINGPOT. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in this state is undecided and subject to change, as when planning is still under way.

clue.text: St Paul, perhaps, given mauling by reptiles

indicators.note: being mauled leaves the word torn apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An apostle savaged by snakes, recalling Paul and the viper on Malta.
explanation.walkthrough: In Acts, a viper bites Paul on Malta and he is unharmed, which is the surface's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul wrote many of the letters in the New Testament, so he is an example of a letter-writer.

clue.text: Swimmer cramming OU course not worth a great deal

indicators.note: cramming means stuffing one thing into another

parts.note: a tunny is a tuna fish, a swimmer
PPE, philosophy, politics and economics, is a degree course at Oxford University

explanation.surface: A swimmer squeezing in an Open University course that turns out to be of little value.
explanation.walkthrough: OU usually means the Open University, but here it is Oxford University, home of PPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally costing two old pennies, so it means cheap or of little value.

clue.text: Rice dish in which one's found shard of turkey bone

indicators.note: one letter is found inside the dish's name

parts.note: paella is a Spanish rice dish

indicators.note: a shard is a small fragment, here just the first letter

explanation.surface: A fragment of turkey bone turns up in a plate of rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shard of' takes T from 'turkey', which goes into PAELLA.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap is a small bone in front of the knee joint.

clue.text: It flies round the edge

parts.note: a lap is one round of a track
a wing is a side edge, as of a stage or football pitch

explanation.surface: Something speeds around the edge of a track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It flies' is the whole definition: a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This plover is a bird, which is something that flies.

clue.text: 'I like that pub!' (Wife takes part in row)

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house
an oar is a piece of equipment used to row

explanation.surface: Someone praises a pub while their wife joins a row.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang interjection expresses lustful approval, roughly 'I'm impressed by that'.

clue.text: Escape for one up-and-coming gentleman

indicators.note: in a down clue the letters come upwards, so read them backwards

parts.note: eg means for example, for one
a toff is an upper-class gentleman

explanation.surface: An ambitious young gentleman manages to escape.
explanation.definitionFit: To get away with something or avoid punishment, a phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Basically having a tip cut from number one read on energy

parts.note: number one is a childish word for urinating
PTO, please turn over, tells you to read on
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone keeps reading a passage about a tip at a basic level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basically' means at the base, the foot: the shoe has its toe tip cut away.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe with an opening at the front lets the toes show, as if the tip were cut off at the bottom.

clue.text: Perhaps Peter Pan s growing up … good heavens, no!

indicators.note: in a down clue growing up means the letters rise, reading bottom to top

parts.note: my is an exclamation of surprise
nope is slang for no

explanation.surface: The boy who never grows up is horrified at the thought of doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray 's' after 'Pan' simply links definition to wordplay; 'growing up' suits Peter Pan, who famously never grows up.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Pan is a title character whose name gives the play its name, an example of a name-giver.

clue.text: Why let them in too? Cast of actors continue in dressing room

indicators.note: a cast is a new mould, so the letters of the question are formed into a new shape

explanation.surface: A director asks why extra performers were let in, then tells the troupe to carry on getting ready.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from Leoncavallo's opera Pagliacci, where the clown must put on his costume and go on with the show.
explanation.definitionFit: A clown's cry to don the costume and get on with the performance, an instruction to carry on.

clue.text: See 1
See 7
It's locked in by the gates to the upper floor

indicators.note: read toward the upper, the start, so the letters run backwards
letters locked in by words are concealed within them

explanation.surface: Something shut in behind gates that lead upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locked in by' finds EGATE inside 'the gates', and 'to the upper' turns it back.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a storey of a building is used in English for a floor or level.

clue.text: Fine organisation in 1st Avenue building ditch, not peculiar

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
UN is the United Nations organisation
First Avenue is in New York, NY, where the UN headquarters stands
a ha-ha is a sunken ditch serving as a hidden boundary fence

explanation.surface: A fine imposed on a body that is digging a trench outside its First Avenue headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunk fence found in British country estates. The phrase contrasts the two senses of funny: amusing versus strange.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom distinguishes the amusing sense from the odd one, so it means comic rather than strange.
